title: Causes and development across the lifespan
blurb: Sort causes of learning disability by when they act, and plan for changing needs from childhood transition to older age.
question: Denise, 60, has a moderate learning disability and lives with her brother. At her annual health check he mentions she now coughs during meals and often does not answer when called from another room. Which guidance applies, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: A learning disability happens when something affects the brain while it is still developing: before birth, during birth or in early childhood. Causes include genetic conditions, illness in pregnancy, problems around birth such as lack of oxygen, and childhood illness or injury such as meningitis. In plain English: something interrupted the brain's development. For many people, no cause is ever found, and support is based on needs, not on the cause.

items.label: Genetic conditions, maternal illness or infection, alcohol
Lack of oxygen, prematurity, birth trauma
Meningitis, head injury, seizures in early childhood

head: Timing
Example
Nursing link
teach.caption: Classify by when the cause acted, not when the diagnosis was made.

teach.body: A known cause does not change the definition or remove the disability, but it guides care. It points to linked health risks to check for (for example the heart and thyroid in Down syndrome), gives the family information about the chance of it happening again and whether relatives should be offered testing, and links people with condition-specific support. Where no cause is found, the person's needs are assessed and met in the same way.

steps.label: Year 9 (13–14)
steps.sub: Transition planning starts at the latest

steps.label: From 14
steps.sub: Annual health check if on GP register

steps.label: Transfer
steps.sub: Named worker, 6 months before and after

teach.caption: NICE NG43 (transition) and NG96 (growing older with learning disabilities).

teach.body: NICE NG43 says transition planning should start by year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest, with an annual review. A named worker coordinates the move and support continues for at least 6 months before and after transfer. Transfer should happen at a time of relative stability, not on a rigid birthday. Planning covers health, education and work, independent living and community inclusion, with the young person at the centre.

rows.label: Who
values: Young people moving to adult services

teach.body: People with learning disabilities are living longer, and many conditions appear earlier or are missed. NICE NG96 lists age-related conditions to ask about and monitor, including hearing loss and sight problems, dysphagia, epilepsy, thyroid problems, osteoporosis, menopausal symptoms, dementia, diabetes, cancer, incontinence and depression. It also highlights older family carers: plan early with the person and their family, including for emergencies and for what happens if a carer can no longer provide care, so decisions are made before a crisis.

teach.h: Scenario: Denise at her annual health check
teach.body: Denise's new coughing at meals suggests dysphagia, and not answering from another room suggests hearing loss. Both are age-related conditions NICE NG96 says to monitor. The nurse arranges a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment and a hearing test, and records both in her health action plan. She also asks her brother about his own health and future plans, because older family carers need support to plan ahead.

teach.text: Timing is about when the cause acted. Down syndrome is prenatal (genetic) even though it is diagnosed after birth. A brain injury at 25 causes an acquired impairment, not a learning disability, because it happened in adulthood.

items: Prenatal (genetic, maternal illness, alcohol), perinatal (hypoxia, prematurity), postnatal (meningitis, injury).
Many people have no identified cause; support follows needs.
A known cause guides health checks, family information and support.
NG43: plan from year 9 at the latest; named worker; 6 months before and after transfer.
NG96: monitor age-related conditions such as hearing, sight, swallowing, epilepsy, thyroid, bones, menopause and dementia; plan with older carers.

summary: You can now classify causes of learning disability as prenatal, perinatal or postnatal and explain why knowing a cause helps. You can also apply NICE NG43 to transition planning and NICE NG96 to the changing health needs of people growing older with learning disabilities.

A.q: A student is sorting causes of learning disability by timing. Down syndrome is usually diagnosed after birth. How should it be classified?
options: Perinatal, because it is diagnosed around the time of birth
Postnatal, because its features show during infancy
Prenatal, because the extra chromosome is there from conception
Unclassified, because genetic causes form a separate group
A.why: Down syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 21, present from conception, so it is a prenatal (genetic) cause.

whyNot.0: Timing depends on when the cause acted, not when the diagnosis is made.
whyNot.1: Features may become clearer later, but the cause is present before birth.

A.q: A nurse is teaching carers about causes of learning disability. Which is a postnatal cause?
options: Oxygen deprivation during a difficult delivery
Very premature birth with complications
Infection in the mother during early pregnancy
Meningitis in the first year of life
A.why: Postnatal causes act after birth, in early childhood: illnesses such as meningitis, accidents and head injury.

whyNot.0: Oxygen deprivation during delivery is perinatal.
whyNot.1: Complications of premature birth act around the time of birth: perinatal.
whyNot.2: Maternal infection in pregnancy is prenatal.

A.q: After genetic tests and scans, no cause has been found for Ella's learning disability. Her parents ask whether the diagnosis is wrong. What is the most accurate reply?
options: In many people no cause is found, and support is based on her needs
Further genetic testing will find the cause in nearly every case
Without a known cause, the diagnosis needs to be reviewed later
No cause means the disability must have started after birth
A.why: Causes are not always identifiable (NHS). A learning disability is defined by impaired intelligence and social functioning starting in childhood, not by a known cause.

whyNot.1: Many people never have a cause identified, even with extensive testing.
whyNot.2: The definition does not depend on a cause, so the diagnosis stands.
whyNot.3: An unknown cause gives no information about timing.

B.q: Denise, 60, has a moderate learning disability. Her brother says she has started coughing during meals over the last two months. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Puree all her food until the coughing has settled down
Record it as a new behaviour in her support plan
Advise her to sip water between each mouthful of food
Refer her for a speech and language therapy swallow assessment
B.why: Coughing at meals suggests dysphagia, an age-related condition NICE NG96 says to monitor. A speech and language therapist assesses and sets a safe eating and drinking plan.

whyNot.0: Changing food texture without assessment may be wrong for her and delays proper assessment.
whyNot.1: This is a possible physical problem with aspiration risk, not a behaviour.
whyNot.2: Advice without assessment may be unsafe; thin fluids can be harder to swallow.

B.q: Ayo, 13, has a severe learning disability and is in year 8. His mother asks when planning for his move to adult services should begin. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
options: At 17, about six months before the transfer happens
From year 9 at the latest, around age 13 or 14
At 18, when adult services formally take over
At 16, when he completes year 11 at school
B.why: NICE NG43 1.2.1: transition planning should start from year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest.

whyNot.0: Six months is the minimum named-worker support either side of transfer, not the planning start.
whyNot.2: Waiting until 18 is far too late and risks a crisis transfer.
whyNot.3: Year 11 is later than NG43 recommends.

B.q: Rhys, 14, has a moderate learning disability and is on his GP's learning disability register. His father asks whether he can have an annual health check. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, he can have a free annual health check from age 14
Not yet, as checks start when he joins adult services at 18
Not yet, as checks start at 16 at the GP's discretion
Yes, once the community learning disability team refers him
B.why: Anyone aged 14 or over on the GP learning disability register can have a free annual health check (NHS.uk).

whyNot.2: Checks start at 14, not at a GP's discretion at 16.
whyNot.3: No specialist referral is needed; being on the GP register is the gateway.

C.q: Lucy, 17, has PMLD and is moving from children's to adult health services. Her family worry about losing the nurse who coordinates her care. What does NICE NG43 recommend about named worker support?
options: It continues until the day of transfer to adult services
It continues for 3 months after transfer has taken place
It continues for at least 6 months before and after transfer
It runs for one year before transfer and ends at age 18
C.why: NICE NG43 1.2.9: support for at least 6 months before and after transfer, coordinated by a named worker.

whyNot.0: Support should continue after transfer, not stop on the day.
whyNot.1: The minimum after transfer is 6 months, not 3.
whyNot.3: NG43 avoids rigid age thresholds and recommends support after transfer too.

C.q: Brian, 66, has a moderate learning disability and lives with his sister, 79, who has had two hospital admissions this year. Several professionals are involved. Which action follows NICE NG96?
options: Wait for a crisis assessment if his sister becomes unable to cope
Agree a single lead practitioner and plan ahead with both of them
Arrange a care home placement now that Brian is over 65 years old
Transfer Brian's care to the older adults' mental health team
C.why: NICE NG96 recommends a single lead practitioner as point of contact (1.5.7) and proactive planning with the person and older family carers, including for emergencies, before a crisis is reached (1.4.5, 1.4.7).

whyNot.0: Waiting for a crisis is what NG96 aims to prevent.
whyNot.2: Age alone is not a reason for a care home; the plan follows Brian's wishes and needs.
whyNot.3: There is no mental health need described; his learning disability support continues.

C.q: Phil, 40, has a moderate learning disability. After his niece is diagnosed with fragile X syndrome, testing shows Phil has it too. His sister asks what difference the diagnosis makes. What is the most accurate answer?
options: It changes his eligibility for adult social care support
It means his learning disability diagnosis is removed
It allows a cure through targeted gene therapy
It guides health checks and informs relatives about testing
C.why: A known cause guides surveillance for linked conditions (in fragile X: anxiety, seizures) and gives relatives information about inheritance and testing.

whyNot.0: Eligibility depends on needs, not on the cause.
whyNot.1: The cause explains the learning disability; it does not remove it.
whyNot.2: There is no curative gene therapy for fragile X in current practice.

reteach.title: When did the interruption happen?
reteach.question: Imagine brain development as a journey from conception to adulthood. Where on that journey can a learning disability begin, and what changes along the road?

blocks.body: Before birth: the genes or the environment in the womb (Down syndrome, alcohol, infection). Around birth: lack of oxygen, prematurity. After birth: meningitis or a head injury in early childhood. Once adulthood is reached, new brain injury is not a learning disability.

blocks.text: A diagnosis made at age 3 does not make a cause postnatal. Ask when the cause acted.

explain.body: Genetic conditions (Down syndrome, fragile X, Prader-Willi), illness or infection in the mother, and alcohol in pregnancy. They act before birth.

test.q: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder causing a learning disability is classified as which type of cause?
options: Perinatal
Postnatal
Prenatal
Acquired
test.why: Alcohol crosses the placenta and affects the developing brain before birth: a prenatal cause.

whyNot.3: 'Acquired' describes impairment after the developmental period.

explain.body: Problems around the time of birth: lack of oxygen to the brain, prematurity and birth trauma. These often occur with cerebral palsy and epilepsy.

test.q: Which is a perinatal cause of learning disability?
options: An extra copy of chromosome 21
Lack of oxygen during delivery
A head injury at age two
Infection in early pregnancy
test.why: Oxygen deprivation during delivery acts around birth: a perinatal cause.

whyNot.0: This is a genetic, prenatal cause.
whyNot.2: A head injury in childhood is postnatal.

explain.body: Illness or injury in early childhood while the brain is still developing: meningitis, encephalitis, head injury, severe seizures. Impairment from injury in adulthood is not a learning disability.

test.q: Freya, 5, had encephalitis at 18 months and now has a moderate learning disability. How is this cause classified?
options: Postnatal
Perinatal
Prenatal
Acquired in adulthood
test.why: An illness in early childhood, while the brain is still developing, is a postnatal cause.

whyNot.1: It happened many months after birth, not around birth.
whyNot.3: It occurred in early childhood, during development.

explain.body: Transition planning from year 9 at the latest with a named worker (NG43). Annual health checks from 14. In older age, monitor age-related conditions such as hearing, sight, swallowing, epilepsy, thyroid, bones, menopause and dementia, and plan with older carers (NG96).

test.q: Which group of conditions does NICE NG96 advise monitoring as people with learning disabilities grow older?
options: Hearing, sight, swallowing, thyroid and bones
Asthma, eczema, hay fever and food allergy
Anxiety, panic, phobia and sleep walking
Gout, kidney stones, gallstones and hernia
test.why: NG96 1.5.14 lists common age-related conditions to monitor, including hearing loss and sight problems, dysphagia, thyroid problems and osteoporosis, alongside others such as epilepsy and dementia.

whyNot.1: These allergic conditions are not the age-related list in NG96.
whyNot.2: NG96 does include mental health such as depression, but phobias and sleep walking are not on its age-related list.
whyNot.3: These are not the conditions NG96 lists for monitoring.
